extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematics students writing research papers (graduate students, postdocs, faculty preparing manuscripts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing clear, well-organized mathematics research papers, including grammar/style rules and paper organization/metadata. Emphasizes readability for referees and the mathematical audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive apostrophes and plurals
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat collective/irregular possessives specially and do not use apostrophes to form ordinary plurals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: write “the people’s choice” and “the children’s folly” (possessives even though nouns are plural). Do not write plurals like “TLA’s” or “1960’s”; use “TLAs” and “1960s.” Avoid extraneous apostrophes commonly seen in informal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision vs custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance precision in terminology/notation with established custom; prefer terms readers will recognize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may invent more precise terms, but if custom usage is pervasive (e.g., 'World Series') you will likely be misunderstood. Avoid inventing notation/terminology unless it will be intelligible to your audience; see Section 2.4 on terminology and notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject–verb agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure subject and verb agree in number; analyze the root sentence to determine the correct conjugation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: do not write “The set of all morphisms are compact.” Omit modifiers: “The set is compact.” Use the device of focusing on the root statement or breaking into pieces to detect agreement errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear reference (this/that/these/those)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using demonstratives without a clear antecedent; repeat nouns rather than rely on potentially vague pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problematic: “Because of this, we decided that.” Ask 'this what?' and 'decided what?'. Prefer repeating the noun or explicitly stating the referent. When the referent is close the demonstrative may be fine; otherwise repeat for clarity. Copy editor maxim: good writing answers more questions than it raises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dangling 'where' clauses; define before use
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not tack definitions onto the end of statements with clauses like 'where ...'—define terms before you use them and put matters in logical order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad example: “Every convex polynomial function is of even degree, where we define a function to be convex if ...” Instead define 'convex' before the theorem. Push definitions earlier rather than requiring readers to pick them up on the fly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who vs whom; subject vs object pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'who' for subjects and 'whom' (and 'me') for objects; test compound constructions by breaking them into component sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: “The pastor, whom expected a large donation, smiled warmly.” Correct: “The pastor, who expected a large donation, smiled warmly.” Test compound subjects: replace 'Bobby and I' with 'I' and check whether the pronoun should be subject or object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives vs adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use adjectives to modify nouns and adverbs to modify verbs; distinguish and use them correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct: “This is a good book.” “She shouts loudly.” Don't confuse forms. Examples given: 'quick'/'brown' as adjectives modifying 'fox'; 'loudly'/'beautifully' as adverbs modifying verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate vs alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish meanings: 'alternate' implies alternating turns/events; 'alternative' implies a choice between mutually exclusive options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Pierre alternately dated Mimi and Fifi' (alternate). 'He chose the alternative lifestyle' (alternative). Use the correct word to avoid misleading meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb 'to be' and predicate nominatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the verb 'to be' takes a predicate nominative, not an object; prefer 'This is I' in formal usage rather than 'This is me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal correctness: 'This is I' or 'It is I who proved...' rather than 'This is me.' In practice many use 'This is me' conversationally but avoid in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare vs contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'compare' to highlight similarities and 'contrast' to emphasize differences; they serve different rhetorical functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: compare groups and semigroups because both are associative; contrast them because one has inverses and the other does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different from vs different than
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'different from' (classical usage); be consistent in whichever modern allowance you adopt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'His view of grammar is different from mine.' Modern treatments permit 'different than' in some contexts but decide on a usage and be consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'due to', 'because of', 'through'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid wordy or incorrect uses of 'due to' (e.g., 'due to the fact that'); use 'due to' for adjectival clauses, not adverbial clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of thumb (G. Piranian): use 'due to' only to introduce an adjectival clause. Prefer 'because' for causal clauses and avoid 'due to the fact that.' See referenced treatments for full discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farther vs further
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Farther' denotes physical distance; 'further' denotes time, quantity, or metaphorical extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'study further the question' vs 'throw the baseball farther than Ty Cobb.' Maintain precision when distinguishing physical vs figurative distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit your prose to the occasion (good taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Match diction and style to the genre and audience; in mathematics, simpler prose is usually better and flamboyant writing is out of place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate tone (e.g., do not use romantic novel tropes in math writing). Strive for clarity and restraint rather than embellishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hopefully vs I hope
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'hopefully' as a sentence adverb meaning 'I hope'; use it to modify verbs (e.g., 'she looked at him hopefully').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: 'Hopefully the weather will be better today' (meaning 'I hope'). Use 'I hope that the weather...' instead. There are differing views in usage literature, but avoid the sentence-adverb use in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Splitting infinitives
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally avoid splitting infinitives unless splitting yields better meaning or sound; use ear and sense to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: prefer 'to enjoy his food immensely' rather than 'to immensely enjoy.' Modern view permits splitting when necessary for clarity or emphasis; rephrase where possible to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous 'in terms of'
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit unnecessary phrases like 'in terms of' when they add no value; prefer direct questions and phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Who is he, in terms of surname?' Better: 'What is his surname?' Remove flabby expressions for concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of 'only' and 'suffices to'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use constructions like 'We need only show that...' and 'It suffices to show that...' carefully and avoid misplacement of 'only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid incorrect forms such as 'We only need to show that...' or 'Suffices it to show that...'. Overuse also weakens prose; use sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parallel grammatical structures for proximate clauses with similar content or purpose to increase effectiveness and memorability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of strong parallelism: 'Candy is dandy but liquor is quicker.' Use parallel forms to make arguments more forceful and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participial phrases (avoid dangling participles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure participial phrases modify the intended noun; avoid dangling participles that produce illogical modifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Shining like the sun, the man gazed upon the heap of gold coins.' Correct: 'The heap of gold coins, which shone like the sun, was gazed upon by the man' or better rephrasing. Maxim: 'When dangling, don't use participles.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending sentences with prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule avoid ending sentences with prepositions; often the preposition is unnecessary or the sentence can be rephrased more elegantly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'At what point do we stop playing?' to 'Where do we stop playing at?' Often rephrasing (e.g., 'When do we stop playing?') is superior. Be mindful that strict avoidance can lead to awkwardness—use sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation with quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow standard U.S. practice: commas and periods inside quotation marks; colons and semicolons outside; question/exclamation placement depends on context; multi-paragraph quotes open each paragraph with a quote mark and close only at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: As Methuselah used to say, 'When the going gets tough, the tough get going.' Be consistent; publishers and copy editors may have differing rules—be prepared to negotiate. British usage differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbal redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid locally redundant adjectives/phrases (e.g., 'old adage', 'past history', 'advance planning'); use logical redundancy only when it aids teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical redundancy can be a teaching device; local verbal redundancy is ignorant and superfluous. Edit to remove tautologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shall vs will
rubrics_metrics.description: In formal writing, use 'shall' for first-person future; use 'will' for second- and third-person future; use 'will' with first-person to express determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I shall drown...' versus 'I will drown and no one shall save me' (illustrating differing nuance). Understand the formal distinction, though colloquial usage often ignores it.

rubrics_metrics.name: That vs which for restrictive/amplifying clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That' denotes restriction (essential clause); 'which' denotes amplification (nonrestrictive clause); choose according to logical role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical example: 'A holomorphic function that vanishes on S must be identically zero' (restrictive — use 'that'). Modern grammarians permit 'which' in some contexts; sound and sense can sometimes overrule technical strictness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define acronyms and avoid unexplained jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use acronyms or jargon unless you are certain the audience knows them; define the acronym parenthetically on first use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The SALT (Strategic Arms Limitation Talks) were progressing poorly... A few hours later, we resumed our efforts with SALT.' Avoid assuming readers know organizational or field-specific abbreviations—remember international readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informative, specific title
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a title that conveys substantive information about the paper's content so readers can judge relevance at a glance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'On a theorem of Hoofnagel.' Better: 'Quadratic convergence of Lax/Wendroff schemes with optimal estimates on the error term' (tells reader exactly what the paper is about). A good title helps attract readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author name consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a consistent author name across publications to ensure correct retrieval by abstracting and indexing services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a stable form (e.g., S. G. Krantz) and stick with it so databases retrieve all your works. Avoid whimsical or inconsistent name variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include standard technical components
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematics paper should include title, affiliations, postal and e-mail addresses, date, abstract, key words, AMS subject classification numbers, and acknowledgements as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List provided: (1) affiliations, (2) addresses/email, (3) date, (4) abstract, (5) key words, (6) AMS classification numbers, (7) thanks to funding agencies and others. Follow journal-specific instructions about placement (title page vs footnote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose meaningful key words and AMS classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Select specific, descriptive key words and correct AMS codes so indexing services place your paper before the right audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague words like 'new' or 'interesting' as key words; prefer technical descriptors like 'pseudoconvex', 'Cauchy problem', 'exotic cohomologies'. Use the AMS classification scheme to target the correct subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgements etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge helpful conversations, readers of drafts, and mandatory funding sources appropriately; ask permission before thanking someone publicly when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not thank people in advance for presumed helpful referee comments; thanking the referee is best after receiving referee input. Always acknowledge agencies that provided financial support when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductory nontechnical summary and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the paper with a nontechnical summary of main results, history of the problem, prior work, and an outline of the organization so readers can decide whether to read further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong intro tells (i) what the paper is about, (ii) why the result is new, (iii) the context/relations to prior work, and (iv) an outline. This helps attract interested readers and orients referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for the referee and the cautious reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume the referee will fill in gaps; explicitly explain why your theorems are new and interesting and why techniques are original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the introduction and exposition are not persuasive, a referee may conclude the paper is second-rate. Make the novelty and contribution explicit to aid acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize proofs with 'big steps' first and technical details later
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proof sections to present the main steps and how lemmas fit together; defer lengthy technical proofs/details to the end of the paper or appendices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3 (proofs) should give the big picture and formulate technical lemmas, showing how they yield the theorem; push nasty details to the end. This structure lets readers decide how deep to read and reduces reader fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present mathematics in a pedagogically effective order (not strict logical order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize material in a way that aids comprehension (summary, motivation, definitions, main results, proof sketch, then technical details), rather than strictly in logical derivation order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning theory suggests readers understand better when given overview and motivation first. Strict Bourbaki-style logical order may archive results but is less effective for communicating ideas and for broad readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use redundancy judiciously (teaching vs verbosity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ logical redundancy when it aids teaching, but avoid unnecessary verbal redundancy that adds no information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redundancy can help pedagogy—repeat important points for clarity—but avoid tautologies and superfluous adjectives that signal poor editing.
